title: India's Copyright Office Rules AI-Generated Work Can Be Protected, but AI Cannot Be Named Author
excerpt: In a landmark ruling on the DABUS artwork case, India takes a more permissive stance than the United States, holding that AI-generated output can meet originality requirements while restricting authorship to humans.
body:
• India's Copyright Office has ruled that AI-generated work can satisfy the originality requirement under copyright law, but the AI system itself cannot be named as the author — authorship must belong to a human.
  • The ruling came on August 31 in the case of Stephen Thaler's AI system DABUS, which he sought to register as the author of an artwork titled "A Recent Entrance to Paradise."
  • India has taken a more permissive position than the United States, where courts and the Copyright Office refused protection for AI-generated work outright; the US Supreme Court declined Thaler's appeal on March 2, 2026.
  • The decision creates a practical framework: if a human supplies inputs, configures the AI system and initiates the generative process, the resulting work can be copyrighted — with the human as author.

The DABUS Case Reaches India

The Indian Copyright Office on August 31 rejected an application seeking to register an AI system as the author of a copyrighted artwork — but in doing so, it carved out a position significantly more accommodating to AI-generated content than that of the United States.

https://x.com/barandbench/status/2094420244580401653

The case centred on Stephen L. Thaler, an American computer scientist who filed a copyright application in 2022 for an artwork titled "A Recent Entrance to Paradise." Thaler named his AI system DABUS — Device for the Autonomous Bootstrapping of Unified Sentience — as the author, with himself listed as the applicant and publisher.

Registrar of Copyrights Prof. Dr. Unnat P. Pandit rejected the application on the ground that "DABUS is not a natural or juristic person recognised in law and cannot be entered as author under Section 2(d)(vi)" of the Copyright Act, 1957. The application had been pending for nearly four years before the Delhi High Court directed the Copyright Office to conclude proceedings.

The Crucial Distinction

What makes the Indian ruling notable is not the rejection of DABUS as author — that outcome was expected and mirrors decisions in the US, UK and Australia. It is the Copyright Office's finding on the work itself.

The Registrar held that AI-generated work can meet the originality requirement under Indian copyright law. The standard, as articulated in the order, focuses on whether "a legally recognised person supplies and curates the relevant inputs, configures and initiates a non-trivial generative process, and thereby causes an independently generated expressive work to come into existence."

The Copyright Office found that, based on the record, the DABUS artwork "possesses sufficient independently generated expressive character." Had Thaler agreed to name himself as the author — an option he was offered during the hearing — registration could have proceeded. He declined, insisting that DABUS be credited.

"Autonomy in execution is not synonymous with the conception of a work."

— Registrar of Copyrights, Indian Copyright Office

India vs. the United States

The contrast with the American position is stark. In the US, both the Copyright Office and the courts have refused copyright protection for AI-generated work outright. The US Copyright Office has held that copyright requires human authorship, and works generated autonomously by AI do not qualify. The Supreme Court declined to hear Thaler's appeal on March 2, 2026.

India's Section 2(d)(vi) of the Copyright Act provides a different legal foundation. It defines the author of a "computer-generated" work as "the person who causes the work to be created" — language that was enacted decades before generative AI but now offers a framework for accommodating it. The Indian Copyright Office has interpreted this provision to mean that the human who designs, configures and initiates the AI system is the author, not the system itself.

As MediaNama noted, this puts India "somewhere more permissive than the United States," where the output itself is denied protection regardless of how much human effort went into designing the AI system.

An Existing Contradiction

The ruling also surfaces an uncomfortable inconsistency in India's copyright register. An AI-generated painting called "Suryast," created using the RAGHAV AI system, was registered by the Copyright Office in 2020 with the AI listed as a co-author alongside its human developer. That registration remains on the books.

The DABUS order does not address or reconcile this earlier registration, creating a tension that future cases or legislative action will need to resolve.

What This Means for India's Tech and Creative Industries

For India's fast-growing AI industry, the ruling provides practical clarity. Companies and individuals using AI tools to generate images, music, text or code can seek copyright protection for the output — provided a human is named as the author who caused the work to be created. This is a more workable framework than the blanket exclusion adopted in the US.

For the Indian diaspora working in global tech companies, the ruling signals that India may emerge as a more favourable jurisdiction for protecting AI-assisted creative work. As generative AI becomes embedded in design, media and software development, the question of who owns the output — and where it can be protected — will only grow in commercial importance.
